This data model has been developed to represent the wide range of restoration practices employed on the UMRS throughout many years and be adaptable into the future. As we learn lessons about restoration, this data model has evolved along with our best practice.

title: 1  Introduction
text:
UMRS Restoration Data Model

Purpose
The restoration features are GIS feature classes designed to document the key design elements of ecosystem restoration features built on the Upper Mississippi River System (UMRS). This data model has been developed to represent the wide range of restoration practices employed on the UMRS throughout many years and be adaptable into the future. As we learn lessons about restoration, this data model has evolved along with our best practice.


Data Design Standards
The entities in this data model represent the physical structures constructed to accomplish the restoration objectives of each project. These entities are grouped into standardized GIS “feature classes” (groups of objects of single type having a common set of attributes). This standard was adapted from the DOD SDSFIE-V (https://www.sdsfie.mil) to represent the specialized features built on the UMRS. This data model was designed to represent UMRS best practice as documented in the UMRR Design Handbook (2012, 2025).


Data Use

Common Terms - Provides a common lexicon of ecosystem restoration features representing current best practice to streamline communication across a diverse group of stakeholders, spread across many organizations, from many disciplinary backgrounds.
Cartography - Defines a standardized framework for representing a wide variety of complex spatial features on different media types (i.e., static paper maps, interactive web maps). Maps are one of the most effective communication tools to describe project benefits to the public.
Upward Reporting - Expressing these diverse features in a standard framework supports automated summarization to streamline routine upward reporting of project status and benefits.
Record Keeping - Forty years of UMRS restoration has generated a rich set of built features to monitor and learn from. This standardized framework, that can evolve with current best practice, is the best way to track our investments.
Whole Project Lifecycle - This standardized framework allows us to track projects throughout their entire lifecycle, from planning and feasibility, through design and construction, and through operation and maintenance. UMRS Restoration Data Model

text:
Implementation
The Army Corps of Engineers project process typically involves four main phases: pre-study initiation (community request), feasibility study, design and construction, and operation and maintenance.

Feasibility

The Corps conducts a detailed study to assess the problem, evaluate potential solutions, and determine project feasibility.
Analysis includes environmental impacts, economic benefits, and cost-benefit analysis.
Report is submitted to higher authorities for review and approval.



Design & Construction

If the project is approved, detailed design plans are developed.
Necessary permits are obtained.
Construction contracts are awarded and project is built.


Operation and Maintenance
Once completed, the Corps manages the project, including routine maintenance and repairs.

title: 1  Introduction
text:
Current Programs Usage

UMRR
To work within a partnership among federal and state agencies and other organizations; to construct high-performing habitat restoration, rehabilitation projects; to produce state-of-the-art knowledge through monitoring, research, and assessment; to engage other organizations to accomplish the Upper Mississippi River Restoration Program’s vision.
The HREP element has fostered interdisciplinary and collaborative planning for habitat restoration, preservation, and enhancement previously non-existent on any other river system in the United States.


NESP
The Navigation and Ecosystem Sustainability Program (NESP) is a long-term, dual-purpose program that integrates navigation improvements and ecosystem restoration together to provide Upper Mississippi River System once in a generation-type positive impact.
The purpose of the Navigation and Ecosystem Sustainability Program is to improve efficiency and capacity of the nationally significant Upper Mississippi River – Illinois Waterway (UMR-IWW) navigation system while protecting preserving and enhancing the structure, diversity, and function of this nationally significant ecosystem.


Notes
Several ecosystem restoration programs are active on the UMRS at the local, state, and federal levels. This data model was designed to function as a repository of the ecosystem restoration features common within a large river floodplain system such as the UMRS, independent of jurisdiction or funding source.

title: 2  Case Studies
text:
An Integrated Framework in Practice: Detailed Case Studies in USACE Upper Mississippi River Restoration

Introduction: From a Toolkit of Features to Integrated Systems
The ecological restoration of the Upper Mississippi River System (UMRS) is a monumental undertaking guided by the sophisticated methodology outlined in the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers’ (USACE) 2012 UMRR EMP Environmental Design Handbook. While the handbook provides a detailed lexicon of individual “restoration features,” their true power is only realized when they are integrated into a cohesive project designed to address specific, large-scale ecological deficits. To understand this methodology in its practical application, it is best to examine it through the lens of real-world case studies. This chapter will therefore explore the USACE restoration process through four major Habitat Rehabilitation and Enhancement Projects (HREPs). Each section will deconstruct a project to show how a unique combination of primary and supporting features was used to address its specific ecological problems, demonstrating how the abstract toolkit is transformed into functional, resilient, and interconnected ecosystems on the ground.




Case Study 1: The Pool 8 Islands HREP - Geomorphic Restoration for Ecological Resurgence
Project Context and Goal: The Pool 8 Islands HREP, located in the vast Weaver Bottoms area near Brownsville, Minnesota, addressed one of the most significant consequences of river impoundment: the creation of a wide, shallow, lake-like environment. The 4,000-acre backwater suffered from a wind fetch of over two miles, which generated constant wave action. This energy re-suspended fine bottom sediments, leading to extremely high turbidity that blocked sunlight, prevented the growth of vital submerged aquatic vegetation (SAV), and eroded the few remaining natural shorelines. The primary goal was to re-engineer the geomorphology of the pool to reduce wave energy, improve water clarity, and spur the large-scale recovery of the aquatic ecosystem.
Integrated Feature Application in Detail: This project is a classic example of geomorphic restoration centered on the beneficial use of dredged material. The foundational activity was a large-scale Dredge Event, which sourced over 1.5 million cubic yards of clean sand during routine maintenance of the 9-foot navigation channel. This material was then transported and strategically placed to construct a complex of 17 new Islands. The curvilinear, naturalistic layout of these islands was precisely guided by a detailed Island Line survey plan, which provided the exact coordinates for construction crews to place material accurately and create the desired footprint.
The immediate stability of these new sand landforms was critical. To prevent their immediate erosion by the very forces they were designed to block, their exposed, windward shores were armored with a heavy rock Revetment. This involved placing thousands of tons of Class III riprap over a durable geotextile fabric, creating a resilient shield against wave attack that was essential for the project’s long-term survival.
Once the physical forms were stable, a massive Flora Planting or Seeding effort transformed the sterile sand into living habitat. On the highest elevations of the islands, designed to be above the 2-year flood frequency, over 80,000 hardwood trees—including species like swamp white oak, river birch, and pecan—were planted to initiate a floodplain forest. On the lower, marshy benches and shorelines, the substrate was seeded with native grasses and forbs to create a diverse emergent Wetland fringe, providing both erosion control and valuable habitat.
The project’s success was profound. In the protected zones behind the islands, water clarity improved from inches to several feet. This triggered a massive resurgence of SAV, with coverage increasing by hundreds of acres. This, in turn, created a rich nursery and foraging habitat for fish and invertebrates, and a major feeding area for migratory waterfowl. To manage the area and inform the public, numerous Signs were installed. These include kiosks at public access points explaining the project’s success and “Slow No Wake Zone” buoys to protect the fragile, newly established vegetation from boat wakes.



Case Study 2: The Weaver Bottoms (Pool 5) HREP - Large-Scale Drawdown and Geomorphic Control
Project Context and Goal: The Weaver Bottoms project in Pool 5 was another massive HREP aimed at restoring a 4,000-acre backwater that had degraded into a wide, shallow lake with almost no vegetation. Like Pool 8, it suffered from immense wind and wave action. The project had a dual goal: first, to reduce wave energy through physical barriers, and second, to stimulate the germination of the dormant but viable native seed bank that lay buried in the riverbed sediments, a process that required physically dewatering a vast area of the Mississippi River.
Integrated Feature Application in Detail: This complex project combined geomorphic construction with large-scale hydraulic manipulation. Similar to Pool 8, a major Dredge Event sourced material for the construction of several new Islands, including a large, crescent-shaped island, to break up wave fetch and create sheltered zones. However, the most innovative component was a large-scale, partial drawdown of the backwater. This was a significant engineering challenge that required modifying existing Water Control Structures at the outlet of the backwater to release water faster than it was entering. To facilitate the dewatering of such a vast area, targeted Dredging was also performed to create deeper Flow Channels that would act as drainage arteries, ensuring the entire area could dewater effectively as the main pool level was lowered.
The drawdown exposed thousands of acres of mudflats for an entire growing season. This had two key ecological effects: first, it allowed the wet, mucky sediment to dewater and consolidate, creating a firmer substrate. Second, and more importantly, the combination of sunlight and air stimulated the germination of a massive seed bank of native aquatic plants (like wild celery and arrowhead) that had been dormant in the sediment for years. When the area was slowly reflooded the following year, a lush and diverse plant community emerged, transforming the “dead lake” back into a productive marsh. The newly constructed islands, protected by Revetments, provided the long-term wave protection necessary to ensure this newly established vegetation would persist.



Case Study 3: The Swan Lake HREP - Active Management through Complex Infrastructure
Project Context and Goal: The Swan Lake HREP, a vast 10,000-acre floodplain complex on the Illinois River, is one of the most ambitious examples of active habitat management. The site had become disconnected from natural flood pulses, and its wetlands were degraded. The primary goal was to restore a highly productive mosaic of wetland habitats by giving resource managers the ability to control water levels with absolute precision, completely independent of the unpredictable and often ill-timed fluctuations of the river.
Integrated Feature Application in Detail: This project is a masterclass in the integration of supporting infrastructure to achieve an ecological goal. The project’s core is a series of large Moist Soil Management Units (MSUs). This first required the construction of miles of new Embankments, whose alignment was precisely dictated by an Embankment Centerline. The design was a major geotechnical challenge, requiring extensive soil analysis from data collected at dozens of Borehole Points to ensure the embankments would be stable on the soft, alluvial floodplain soils.
The ability to manage water is enabled by several key features. Large, cast-in-place concrete Water Control Structures, fitted with removable stoplogs, were built into the embankments. Because gravity flow was insufficient, several large Pump Stations were constructed, with a combined capacity of over 300 cubic feet per second. This immense power gives managers the ability to fill the vast wetland units from the river in the fall or, critically, to dewater them after an unseasonal summer flood to save the growing food crop.
This operational infrastructure required an equally complex network of utilities and access. A robust electrical grid was installed, consisting of miles of buried armored cable (Electrical Utility Segments) that run along the levee crests. These segments connect the main power grid to the Electrical Utility Nodes—the transformers and motor control panels—located at each remote pump station. A water conveyance network, composed of large-diameter HDPE pipes (Water Utility Segments) and large, wheel-operated gate valves (Water Utility Nodes), moves the massive volumes of water from the pumps to the various wetland cells.
None of this would be possible to build, operate, or maintain without physical access. The project included the construction of several miles of Road Segments on the crests of the main embankments. These roads were surfaced with a thick Pavement Section of compacted aggregate, specifically designed to support the weight of heavy vehicles like cranes and excavators needed for long-term maintenance. The entire construction process was guided by a Feature Stationing system, which provided a linear “address” for every component, allowing for the precise placement of every culvert, pump, and water control structure along the project’s miles of embankments.



Case Study 4: Restoring Connectivity and Complexity - Peoria Lake, Pool 12, and Big Timber HREPs
Project Context and Goal: Many HREPs are not about large-scale geomorphic change but instead focus on more surgical interventions to restore depth, flow, and habitat complexity in degraded backwaters and side channels that have become choked with sediment and cut off from the main river.
Integrated Feature Application in Detail: At the Peoria Lake HREP, the foundational activity was a Dredge Event that removed over 1.3 million cubic yards of sediment to excavate deep channels in the sediment-filled lake. Because the dredged material was fine-grained silt, it was unsuitable for island building and was instead pumped to a designated Dredge Placement site—an adjacent upland containment area where it could be safely dewatered. To bring the newly dredged pools to life, a new Flow Channel was excavated to connect them to the main river, providing a constant supply of fresh water. Within these pools, Fish Structures, including rock piles and anchored logs, were placed to provide immediate habitat complexity for the local fishery.
In Pool 12 of the Mississippi River, the focus was on restoring flow to side channels cut off by historic Riverine Flow Structures (rock wing dikes). Rather than removing the dikes, a more targeted approach was taken. A Notch, typically 30-50 feet wide, was cut into each dike. The design and placement of these notches were guided by a Riverine Flow Structure Line survey plan to ensure they captured the right amount of flow. This allowed a controlled portion of the river’s current to pass through, scouring the side channel and restoring a healthy, flowing environment without compromising the navigation function of the main channel.
Finally, at the Big Timber HREP in Pool 17, managers faced a different problem: the water in the adjacent Mississippi River channel was often too turbid and nutrient-laden to be desirable for their managed wetland. To overcome this, the project included the installation of a high-capacity Well. This feature drills deep into the alluvial aquifer to provide a source of clean, clear, sediment-free groundwater. The well gives managers a critical tool to fill the wetland with high-quality water, allowing them to achieve their vegetation goals even when the river itself is not a suitable water source.

title: 3  Restoration Features Summary
text:
The Integrated Design of River Restoration Features
The “2012 UMRR EMP Environmental Design Handbook” outlines a comprehensive and integrated approach to river restoration, where a diverse suite of features are designed to work together to achieve large-scale ecological uplift in the Upper Mississippi River System. The relationship between the individual restoration features and the overarching design practices is not linear but rather a complex, synergistic web. The core design practice is to view the river not as a series of isolated problems but as a complete ecosystem. Therefore, projects combine multiple features to mimic natural processes, restore habitat, and ensure the long-term resilience of the restored environment.
The restoration features can be broadly understood in two categories: Primary Ecological Features and the Supporting Engineering and Infrastructure Features that enable them. The design practice involves layering these two categories to create a functional and sustainable project.

Primary Ecological Features: The Building Blocks of Restoration These features are the visible, direct interventions aimed at restoring ecological structure and function. Design practices for these features focus on creating specific habitats and restoring natural river processes.


Objective: Enhancing Aquatic Habitat & Connectivity

Features Used: Dredge Events are a cornerstone practice to restore depth in sediment-filled backwaters. This creates overwintering refugia for fish and improves flow. The design is not simply about digging a hole; it involves creating varied depths and complex shapes. To further enhance this, Fish Structures (like rock piles and log snags) are added to provide cover. Flow Channels and Notches in dikes are engineered to reintroduce vital, oxygenated water from the main channel into these restored backwaters, preventing stagnation.
Relationship to Design: The design practice here is one of habitat layering. A single backwater dredging project is designed in concert with flow introduction and in-stream cover to create a complete, multi-faceted aquatic habitat, rather than just a deep pool.

Objective: Restoring Landforms and Floodplain Dynamics

Features Used: Islands, often built using material from Dredge Events (a key synergy), are a primary tool. Their design is strategic: they act as barriers to reduce wind and wave erosion in backwaters, creating sheltered zones for aquatic plants to grow. The islands themselves are designed with varied topography, using Flora Planting and Seeding to establish Floodplain Forests and provide secure nesting habitat.
Relationship to Design: The design practice is geomorphic restoration. It’s not just about building an island, but about using that island as a tool to reshape the river’s flow, energy, and light conditions to benefit the wider ecosystem. The island’s design (shape, elevation, vegetation) is dictated by these broader goals.

Objective: Managing Riparian and Wetland Zones

Features Used: Moist Soil Management Units (MSUs) and Wetlands are created or restored using Embankments to impound water. The key design practice is the precise management of water levels, which is accomplished using Water Control Structures, Pump Stations, and Wells. By controlling the timing and duration of flooding and drawdowns, managers can stimulate the growth of specific native plants that provide critical food for migratory waterfowl.
Relationship to Design: This demonstrates the practice of active ecological management. The features are designed not as static elements, but as a dynamic, controllable system that allows managers to adapt to environmental conditions and meet specific ecological targets year after year.



Supporting Engineering and Infrastructure Features: The Foundation of Success These features are the critical engineering components that make the primary ecological restorations possible, stable, and accessible. The design practice is to integrate these robust engineering solutions seamlessly to ensure the project’s longevity and functionality.


Geotechnical and Structural Stability: A Revetment (rock armor) is designed to protect a newly built Island from eroding. The design of a massive Embankment relies entirely on data from Borehole Points to understand the soil’s capacity to support the structure. Riverine Flow Structures like wing dikes are designed based on extensive hydraulic modeling to ensure they steer river currents effectively without causing unintended erosion elsewhere.
Construction and Operational Logistics: The entire system is built upon a framework of civil infrastructure. Feature Stationing, Embankment Centerlines, and Island Lines provide the precise survey control needed for construction. Road Segments and Pavement Sections are designed to provide all-weather access for heavy machinery during construction and for long-term maintenance and monitoring.
Power and Utilities: The active management of an MSU is impossible without a reliable Pump Station, which in turn depends on a network of Electrical Utility Nodes and Segments. The design practice here ensures that this critical infrastructure is itself resilient, often elevated above flood levels to maintain operational capacity during high-water events.


Conclusion
In summary, the relationship between restoration features and design practices is one of interdependence and synergy. The design process for a UMRR EMP project begins with a clear ecological objective, such as improving fish habitat or restoring a floodplain forest. To achieve this, a suite of primary ecological features are selected and designed as an interconnected system. Finally, this system is built upon a robust foundation of supporting engineering and infrastructure features, which are designed to ensure the primary features are constructed correctly, remain stable over their design life, and can be actively managed to maximize their ecological benefits. No single feature stands alone; its design is always considered in the context of the entire project and the broader river ecosystem.

title: 4  Restoration Features
text:
Restoration Features

DredgingEvent (polygon) – The extent of the area subject to dredging action. (area of material removal)
Embankment (polygon) – The centerline of an embankment for controlling the waters of the sea, river, or other water bodies.
EmbankmentCenterline (line) – The centerline of an embankment for controlling the waters of the sea, river, or other water bodies.
FishStructure (polygon) – An engineered structure designed to improve fish habitat or allow improved fish movement through the river system.
FloraPlantingOrSeeding (polygon) – A location where vegetation is planted or seeded.
FlowChannel (polygon) – An excavated channel (via mechanical or hydraulic means) intended to allow for the flow of water across, into, or out of the project area or any subcomponent of a project area.
Island (polygon) – Island structures engineered with a variety of techniques and materials that serve as barriers to flow, wind and waves.
IslandLine (line) – Island structures engineered with a variety of techniques and materials that serve as barriers to flow, wind and waves.
MoistSoilMgmtUnits (polygon) – Areas or units designed to enhance wetland habitat through the use of water containment, water supply and water control structures.
Notch (point) – A notch in a riverine flow structure (typically a dike) used to control the flow of water into and out of the low flow area.
PumpStation (point) – A location where a pump is located to pump water from the interior of a levee.
Revetment (polygon) – An area faced with stone or other material along the shoreline designed to stabilize the bank or protect it from erosion.
RiverineFlowStructureLine (line) – A natural or man-made flow (or sediment) control structure in a water course or water body such as a dike or weir. This feature should not be used to model a levee.
RiverineFlowStructure (polygon) – A natural or man-made flow (or sediment) control structure in a water course or water body such as a dike or weir. This feature should not be used to model a levee.
WaterControlStructure (point) – A structure designed to allow flow through an embankment.
Well (point) – A shaft dug or drilled into the Earth for the purpose of extracting fluids from the subsurface, collecting environmental samples, injecting fluids into the subsurface or extracting contamination or other impurities from the subsurface.
Wetland (polygon) – Geospatial feature composed of one unique wetland class (no complexes) used to determine USACE jurisdiction and regulatory impacts.

title: 5  Dredging Event
text:
Geometry Type: Polygon (Dredge_Event_Area).
Spatial Delineation: Extents of authorized aquatic cut prisms within backwater lakes, secondary chutes, side channels, access cuts, and sediment deflection basins.
Vertical Bounds: Existing hydrographic bathymetric profile down to engineered project design grade, including allowable design overdepth tolerance (+0.5 to +1.0 ft).
Primary Restoration & Engineering Objectives Overwintering Fish Refugia: Deepen degraded shallow backwaters to restore minimum safe thermal depths (≥8.0 to 10.0 ft) beneath winter river ice cover.
Riverine Velocity Dissipation: Provide low-velocity resting basins (<0.05 ft/s) protected from cold, turbulent main-stem drafts.
Aquatic Habitat Longevity: Calculate design dredge depths using long-term historic bathymetric sedimentation rates to guarantee a minimum 25- to 50-year biological lifespan before re-shoaling.


Typical Cross-Sections, Dimensions & Sizing Criteria

Bottom Widths: Primary fish cuts span 50 to 150 ft; deep winter holes span 100 to 300 ft.
Side Slopes: Typically specified at 1V:3H to 1V:5H in unconsolidated alluvial sands, and 1V:6H to 1V:10H in soft cohesive lacustrine silts.
Target Water Depths: Maintained at 8.0 to 12.0 ft below flat low navigation pool elevation.



Construction & Implementation Methodology

Hydraulic Cutterhead Dredging: Slurry pumping (12 to 24 in pipelines) utilized when material is targeted for long-distance transport into confined disposal facilities (CDFs) or island containment berms.
Mechanical Clamshell / Excavator Dredging: Barge-mounted long-reach excavators and scows utilized when sediments are coarse sand or placed immediately along adjacent island cores.
Turbidity Controls: Silt curtains, hydraulic velocity dissipators, and continuous down-drift total suspended solids (TSS) and dissolved oxygen (DO) monitoring.



Quality Control, Inspection & Long-Term Maintenance

Pre- and Post-Dredge Hydrographic Surveys: Multi-beam and dual-frequency single-beam acoustic sonar runs tied to USACE River Gages and NAVD88 vertical datum.
Long-Term Monitoring: Bathymetric transects established at 200-ft intervals, surveyed at 1-, 3-, 5-, and 10-year intervals post-construction to quantify sediment accretion rates.

title: 5  Dredging Event
text:
Spatial Feature Attribute

Definition
Backwater dredging typically consists of dredging channels with fingers (dredged channels that extend out away from the main dredge cut). The depth and size (length and width) of the dredge cut depends on several site specific factors.


Purpose
Sediment is dredged to create depth diversity in the backwaters can be used to enhance aquatic areas with islands or terrestrial areas with increase topographic diversity, which promotes the growth of mast trees.


Applicability
Many Upper Mississippi River System (UMRS) backwaters have been degraded by excessive amounts of sediment emanating from the basin, tributaries, and mainstem sources. This degradation is in the form of loss of depth, poor sediment quality, poor water quality, and sediment resuspension that blocks light required by aquatic plants. Streambank erosion throughout the basin is another important source of sediment that fills the backwaters. (UMRR Design Handbook, 2012)


Notes
Restoration features now have a Program_UID field to distinguish between NESP and UMRR features. Aliases without program identification will be created for any field that currently has UMRR in the name, so they can be used for NESP or UMRR data.
Attribute criteria for each field includes the following:

Attribute Status – defines whether the field requires a value or if it is optional based on available information.
Phases – indicates the earliest time in the project lifecycle values for this attribute as available.
Digitizing requirements – indicates when the field value should be entered in the attribute table.

Geometry Note: Polygon nodes should have z values; elevations should be taken from as-built survey or design documents.

(polygon) – The extent of the area subject to dredging action. (area of material removal)

title: 6  Embankment
text:
Geometry Type: Polygon (Embankment_Footprint).
Spatial Delineation: Terrestrial earthen footprint bounded by the outer intersection lines of outer fill slopes with native subgrade alluvium.
Functional Roles: Isolating moist soil units, containing perimeter dredged placement cells, protecting wetlands from catastrophic river flood surges, and providing heavy maintenance vehicle access.


Primary Restoration & Engineering Objectives

Hydraulic Isolation: Retain or exclude river floodwaters to facilitate independent moisture and pool-depth management.
Controlled Overtopping Resistance: Engineered to withstand controlled, non-catastrophic submergence during 10- to 25-year flood recurrence events.
Containment Integrity: Form stable retention dikes capable of impounding fine dredged hydraulic slurries without slope shear failures.



Typical Cross-Sections, Dimensions & Sizing Criteria

Crest Width: 10.0 to 14.0 ft for maintenance roadways; 8.0 ft for non-vehicular perimeter berms.
Side Slopes: Interior slopes at 1V:3H to 1V:4H; riverward exterior slopes at 1V:4H to 1V:6H to mitigate wind-wave runup.
Structural Core: Central compacted low-permeability cohesive clay core (CL/CH) with a minimum 3.0-ft bottom cutoff trench keyed into native impermeable strata.
Freeboard: Minimum 2.0 to 3.0 ft above maximum managed impoundment pool stage.



Construction & Implementation Methodology

Subgrade Preparation: Stripping topsoil and organic muck (6 to 18 in); proof-rolling subgrade with heavy vibratory compactors.
Lift Placement & Compaction: Clay and silty-clay fill spread in loose horizontal lifts of 8.0 in maximum, compacted to ≥95% of Standard Proctor Maximum Dry Density (ASTM D698) within ±2% of optimum moisture.
Slope Armoring: Class I to Class II rock riprap placed over non-woven geotextile on exterior wave faces; native perennial root mats established on interior slopes.



Quality Control, Inspection & Long-Term Maintenance

Geotechnical Monitoring: Piezometer installations along toe lines to monitor phreatic water lines and internal seepage gradients.
Routine Inspection: Quarterly inspections for burrowing animals (muskrats/beavers), desiccation cracking, mechanical rutting, and woody tree encroachment along levee toes.

title: 7  Embankment Centerline
text:
Geometry Type: Polyline (Embankment_Centerline_Line).
Spatial Delineation: Longitudinal survey axis running along the geometric centroid of the top crest of the embankment prism.
Data Fields: Linear stationing (0+00), top-of-crest design profile elevation, horizontal curve radii, design freeboard height, and crest width domain codes.


Primary Restoration & Engineering Objectives

Engineering Geometry Control: Serves as the master horizontal and vertical control baseline for all construction layout, cross-sectional cut/fill grading, and post-settlement monitoring.
Profile Consistency: Establishes the uniform, non-dip crest grade to ensure overtopping occurs exclusively at designated, armored spillway notches rather than across unprotected earthen crest segments.



Typical Cross-Sections, Dimensions & Sizing Criteria

Survey Baseline: Stationing established at 100-ft linear increments with permanent control monuments positioned at Points of Curvature (PC) and Points of Tangency (PT).
Grade Tolerances: Construction grade tolerance along centerline is strict: −0.00 ft/+0.20 ft from contract design profile.



Construction & Implementation Methodology

RTK-GPS & Total Station Layout: Field staked with high-precision RTK-GPS tied directly into national State Plane Coordinates (NAD83) and NAVD88 elevation benchmarks.
Machine Control Integration: Centerline coordinate and profile strings loaded into 3D GPS machine-guidance earthmoving excavators and motor graders.



Quality Control, Inspection & Long-Term Maintenance

Settlement Monitoring: Permanent brass survey disks embedded in concrete surface monuments every 500 ft along the centerline, surveyed annually to track long-term primary consolidation of underlying river silts.

text: Spatial & Geometric Definition

title: 8  Fish Structure
text:
Geometry Type: Point or Polygon (Fish_Structure_Location).
Spatial Delineation: Precise spatial coordinates or bounding footprints of submerged structural habitat units embedded in backwater cuts, secondary channels, and plunge basins.
Component Typology: Anchored large woody debris (LWD) complexes, rootwad revetments, brush bundles, boulder clusters, and wooden crib reefs.


Primary Restoration & Engineering Objectives

Cover & Velocity Shelters: Create localized zones of zero velocity (0.0 ft/s) alongside predatory feeding seams for gamefish species (largemouth bass, bluegill, black crappie, walleye).
Macroinvertebrate Substrate: Provide durable, non-silt-covered hard biological surfaces for net-spinning caddisflies, mayflies, and epilithic periphyton.
Thermal Microhabitats: Maintain localized deep cover within overwintering basins, preventing schooling fish from expending critical winter energy reserves.



Typical Cross-Sections, Dimensions & Sizing Criteria

Boulder Clusters: Groups of 3 to 7 interlocking Class IV–V boulders (d 50 =24 to 36 in), placed in staggered diamond formations spanning 15×25 ft footprints.
Rootwad / Tree Deflectors: Hardwood tree trunks (≥18 in diameter) with intact root fans (6 to 10 ft diameter), projecting 10 to 20 ft from channel margins.
Ballast Requirements: Stone ballast sizing calculated to offset submerged wood buoyancy by a factor of safety FS≥1.75 (1.5 to 2.0 tons of rock per full-size tree bole).



Construction & Implementation Methodology

Barge-Mounted Crane Placement: Lowered into aquatic cuts using cable chokers or mechanical clamshells.
Anchoring Systems: Hardwoods secured to riverbeds using duckbill earth anchors, helical steel ground screws, or heavy galvanized aircraft cables (3/8 in diameter) clamped through drilled stone anchors.



Quality Control, Inspection & Long-Term Maintenance

Underwater Acoustic Surveys: High-resolution multi-beam side-scan sonar runs conducted at 2- and 5-year intervals to verify structural presence, orientation, and absence of silt smothering.
Biological Electrofishing: Annual fisheries index surveys comparing fish density at structure sites against un-structured control reaches.

text: Spatial & Geometric Definition

title: 9  Flora Planting Seeding
text:
Geometry Type: Polygon (Flora_Planting_Area).
Spatial Delineation: Managed zones receiving revegetation treatments across restored island crests, moist soil units, dredge disposal sites, and riparian forest floodplains.
Vegetation Types: Hard-mast bottomland hardwoods, native emergent wetland tubers/plugs, pollinator forb mixes, and deep-rooted native warm-season prairie grasses.


Primary Restoration & Engineering Objectives

Soil Bio-Stabilization: Rapid root-mesh development to anchor sandy and fine-grained dredged placement materials against wave-wash and flood shear stress.
Wildlife Mast Production: Re-establish critical hard-mast forest species (swamp white oak, pin oak, shellbark hickory, pecan) displaced by altered post-dam hydrologic regimes.
Invasive Species Suppression: Establish continuous native vegetative cover to prevent colonization by monotypic reed canary grass (Phalaris arundinacea).



Typical Specifications, Densities & Seed Mixes

Hard-Mast Tree Stock: Root Production Method (RPM) or bare-root containerized saplings (1.0-gal to 3.0-gal pots, ≥0.5 in caliper). Planted at densities of 200 to 300 stems/acre on 12×12 ft to 15×15 ft grids.
Riparian Seed Mixes: Native cool- and warm-season grasses (Virginia wildrye, river bulrush, cordgrass, bluejoint grass) broadcast at 10 to 20 lbs Pure Live Seed (PLS)/acre.
Emergent Wetlands: Bare-root tubers/plugs of Sagittaria latifolia and Scirpus fluviatilis installed along littoral margins (0.5 to 2.0 ft water depth) on 3-ft centers.



Construction & Implementation Methodology

Site Preparation: Multi-pass forestry mowing followed by aquatic-approved glyphosate herbicide treatments to eradicate invasive root mats.
Shelter Tube Installation: Hardwood saplings protected with 48- to 60-in rigid, ventilated photodegradable polyethylene tree shelters staked with rot-resistant white oak stakes to eliminate deer browse and rodent girdling.



Quality Control, Inspection & Long-Term Maintenance

Survival Censuses: Fixed-radius inventory plots (0.1 acre) evaluated at months 12, 24, and 36 post-planting. Target standard is ≥80% survival density.
Herbicide Touch-Ups: Backpack spot-spraying or mechanical brush-cutting around tree collars for 3 consecutive growing seasons until sapling crowns overtop competing weeds.

title: 10  Flow Channel
text: Spatial & Geometric Definition

title: 10  Flow Channel
text:
Geometry Type: Polygon (Flow_Channel_Footprint).
Spatial Delineation: Channel boundaries of excavated aquatic chutes, secondary conveyance corridors, or backwater flow-supply corridors reconnecting the main river to isolated interior wetlands.
Hydraulic Classification: Continuous low-velocity flow channels, seasonal skimming channels, or flood pulse distributors.


Primary Restoration & Engineering Objectives

Oxygenated Water Delivery: Introduce low volumes of oxygen-rich river water into stagnant interior backwaters to prevent winter and summer anoxic fish kills.
Biological Corridor Connectivity: Provide passage routes for migratory riverine fish traveling between river feeding reaches and sheltered nursery lakes.
Controlled Energy Conveyance: Route discharge without inducing bed scour, toe destabilization, or excessive sediment imports into fragile interior basins.



Typical Cross-Sections, Dimensions & Sizing Criteria

Bottom Widths: 20 to 60 ft; side slopes stabilized at 1V:3H or flatter.
Longitudinal Bed Slope: Very flat gradient (S≤0.0002 to 0.0005) to constrain cross-sectional average velocities beneath critical erosive limits (v≤1.0 to 1.5 ft/s).
Inlet Control Sills: Hard-armored rock sills placed at the channel inlet set 0.5 to 1.5 ft above normal pool to block bedload sediment entry during low-water regimes.



Construction & Implementation Methodology

Excavation Fleet: Low-ground-pressure (LGP) amphibious excavators or spud-barge mechanical dredge rigs working from downstream upstream to maintain positive gravity dewatering.
Bank Armor Integration: Riprap placement along channel entrance mouths and sharp bendway curves subject to centrifugal shear forces.



Quality Control, Inspection & Long-Term Maintenance

Acoustic Flow Gauging: Seasonal ADCP velocity transects to confirm flow splits match calibrated hydrodynamic model predictions (typically 1% to 5% of main river discharge).
Debris Clearance: Annual post-flood inspection to clear lodged drift logs and alluvial sand wedges from channel entrances.

title: 10  Flow Channel

Definition
A FlowChannel is an excavated channel, created by mechanical or hydraulic means, intended to allow the flow of water across, into, or out of the project area or any subcomponent of a project area.

Flow channels are constructed to direct, convey, or redistribute water in support of restoration objectives. They can be used to reconnect floodplains or backwaters, improve circulation, manage water levels, enhance habitat connectivity, and reduce stagnant or low-quality water conditions by providing designed flow paths.

Flow channels are applicable wherever controlled or enhanced conveyance of water is needed within Upper Mississippi River System (UMRS) restoration projects. They are used in both terrestrial and aquatic settings to route water between project features (e.g., MSMUs, backwater lakes, side channels), restore or mimic natural flow patterns, and support habitat, sediment, and water quality objectives. title: 11  Island Centerline
text:
Geometry Type: Polyline (Island_Crest_Line or Island_Baseline).
Spatial Delineation: Centerline axis, design baseline, or high-crest ridge running continuously along the longitudinal alignment of a constructed island.
Data Fields: Island segment ID, design crest profile grade, baseline stationing, revetment armoring class, and design overtopping threshold.


Primary Restoration & Engineering Objectives

Survey Baseline Control: Serves as the primary reference vector from which cross-sectional design offset templates (perpendicular cross-sections) are generated and staked.
Hydraulic Ridge Integrity: Tracks the continuous elevation of the island’s primary windbreak and flood-deflection backbone.



Typical Specifications & Geometric Properties

Stationing System: Formatted identically to civil alignments (0+00 to L), with stationing typically progressing from the downstream trailing tip to the upstream prow.
Elevation Control: Tied strictly to the project vertical control network (NAVD88) with construction staking tolerances of ±0.1 ft.



Construction & Implementation Methodology

GPS Navigation Strings: Exported as civil design alignment files into real-time barge GPS tracking suites to guide placement derrick operators and bulldozer operators.



Quality Control, Inspection & Long-Term Maintenance

Crest Profile Resurveys: Periodic RTK-GPS profile walks along the island line following major flood inundation cycles to calculate post-consolidation subgrade settlement.

title: 11  Island Centerline
text:
Spatial Feature Attribute

Definition
IslandLine represents the linear footprint or alignment of an island or island segment within a river or backwater area when the feature is too narrow or detailed to be mapped effectively as a polygon at project scale. It captures the engineered or restored island crest or centerline used for analysis, design reference, or cartographic depiction.


Purpose
IslandLine features are used to represent long, narrow, or small island structures where polygon mapping is impractical, while still documenting their location, extent, and functional role in influencing flow, wave action, and habitat conditions. They provide a simplified linear representation that can be used in hydraulic analysis, design layouts, and monitoring of island performance over time.


Applicability
IslandLine is applicable where island features are present but are either too small to digitize as polygons at the project mapping scale or where a linear representation (e.g., crest line, centerline, or control alignment) is needed for modeling, design, or management. Typical uses include narrow barrier islands, training-island alignments, or thin island ridges within Upper Mississippi River System (UMRS) restoration projects. (UMRR Design Handbook, 2012)

title: 12  Island
text:
Geometry Type: Polygon (Restoration_Island_Polygon).
Spatial Delineation: Subaerial landmass polygon constructed above normal flat pool within broad, shallow river expanses.
Architectural Typology: Barrier islands, multi-island archipelagos, horseshoe bays, and interior spits.


Primary Restoration & Engineering Objectives

Wind-Wave Fetch Reduction: Break wind-wave generation across shallow open bays, reducing bottom orbital wave resuspension and restoring water clarity for submersed aquatic vegetation (SAV).
Terrestrial Habitat Creation: Provide secure, predator-isolated nesting habitat for migratory waterfowl, shorebirds, turtles, and bottomland hardwood trees.
Sediment Trapping: Create sheltered leeward lagoons that promote fine sediment drop-out and organic soil building.



Typical Cross-Sections, Dimensions & Sizing Criteria

Crest Elevations: Tiered multi-level profiles:
High Ridges (5 to 10 ft above pool): Designed above the 10- to 25-year flood stage to preserve terrestrial flood refugia and bottomland hardwood mast forests.
Low Sills / Wetland Benches (1 to 3 ft above pool): Frequently overtopped to sustain emergent marsh fringes.
Base Widths & Footprints: Base widths of 100 to 400 ft; total individual footprints ranging from 2 to 50+ acres.
Side Slopes: Windward wave-impact faces sloped at 1V:3H to 1V:4H; leeward slopes shaped gently at 1V:8H to 1V:20H down to shallow littoral shelves.



Construction & Implementation Methodology

Material Sourcing & Sequencing: Fine to medium granular dredged sand mechanically or hydraulically placed to form the structural core.
Cohesive Topsoil Caps: Capping the sand core with a 1.0- to 2.0-ft layer of fine-grained cohesive dredge silt/clay to support plant rooting and resist wind deflation.
Windward Revetment Placement: Placing non-woven geotextile and Class II–III riprap along exposed upstream and windward shorelines concurrently with fill operations.



Quality Control, Inspection & Long-Term Maintenance

Topographic Lidar & RTK Surveys: Post-construction as-built terrain modeling to verify settled elevations against contract cut/fill balances.
Shoreline Stability Audits: Biannual visual inspections to detect riprap displacement, wave notch cutting, or flank erosion following major spring river floods.

title: 12  Island
text:
Spatial Feature Attributes

Definition
Island features are engineered or restored landforms within a river or backwater area, constructed or modified using a variety of techniques and materials to provide physical barriers to flow, wind, and waves, and to support habitat and geomorphic functions.


Purpose
The loss of islands in the Upper Mississippi River is primarily due to human-induced alterations to the river’s natural hydrology and sediment dynamics. Dams, channelization, sediment loss, and altered floodplain connectivity have disrupted the processes that create and maintain islands. As a result, islands are increasingly vulnerable to erosion, lack of sediment deposition, and other environmental stresses, leading to their gradual disappearance. This loss impacts biodiversity and the overall health of the river ecosystem, emphasizing the need for restoration and management efforts to protect and rebuild these important habitats. Island creation serves to restore structural diversity, reduce wave and current energy, improve sediment processes, and provide critical habitat for fish, wildlife, and plants.


Applicability
Island creation serves to restore and enhance river ecosystems, providing diverse habitats for wildlife, improving sediment and water quality processes, supporting floodplain and aquatic species health, and promoting biodiversity. Islands can be incorporated into restoration designs to protect shorelines, create sheltered backwaters, influence flow paths, and support vegetation and nesting habitat. (UMRR Design Handbook, 2012)


Notes
Restoration features now have a Program_UID field to distinguish between NESP and UMRR features. Aliases without program identification will be created for any field that currently has UMRR in the name, so they can be used for NESP or UMRR data.

title: 13  Moist Soil Management Unit
text: Spatial & Geometric Definition

title: 13  Moist Soil Management Unit
text:
Geometry Type: Polygon (MSU_Cell_Boundary).
Spatial Delineation: Enclosed, impounded floodplain basin bounded by perimeter containment embankments, internal ditches, and water control structures.
Ecological Classification: Shallow seasonally flooded palustrine emergent wetland complex.


Primary Restoration & Engineering Objectives

Targeted Seed & Tuber Production: Provide precise, independent hydrologic drawdowns and reflooding to stimulate high-energy forage plants (smartweeds, wild millets, sedges, sprangletop).
Migratory Waterfowl Refueling: Provide shallow foraging water depths (2.0 to 8.0 in) timed precisely to match spring and autumn waterfowl migration pulses.
Shorebird Staging Flats: Expose extensive mudflats during late summer (July–August) for migrating northbound and southbound shorebirds.

title: 13  Moist Soil Management Unit
text:
Typical Cross-Sections, Dimensions & Sizing Criteria

Cell Surface Areas: Individual management cells typically scale from 10 to 80 acres.
Topographic Grading: Graded with gentle interior slopes (<0.1% grade) toward a central drainage swale network (bottomwidths10 to 20 ft) to ensure complete gravity drainage without water pocketing.
Operating Depth Envelope: Maximum impounded water depth of 1.5 to 3.0 ft; drawdowns expose 100% of cell floor to atmospheric drying.


Construction & Implementation Methodology

Precision Earthmoving: Laser-guided bulldozers and low-ground-pressure earthmovers shaping interior swales and cell bottom micro-topography.
Clay Liner Compaction: Where underlying alluvium contains excessive sand lenses, interior floors are sealed with a compacted 1.0- to 2.0-ft cohesive clay blanket to prevent downward water loss.



Quality Control, Inspection & Long-Term Maintenance

Annual Water Management Plans: Rigorous hydro-period cycling: slow spring drawdowns (March–May), summer soil drying and germination (June–August), and gradual fall re-flooding (September–November).
Discing & Succession Setback: Rotational tractor discing or controlled burning every 3 to 5 years to reset plant succession and eliminate monotypic willow or cattail stands.

Spatial Feature Attributes ### Definition Areas or units designed to enhance wetland habitat through the use of water containment, water supply, and water control structures.


Purpose
The basic operating plan for a Moist Soil Management Unit (MSMU) is to keep water out in the late spring and summer and to gradually flood the area in the fall. In a multiple-cell system, independent control of water levels in each cell is preferred to allow targeted habitat management.


Applicability
Moist Soil Management Units are typically designed to include water containment, water supply, and water control structures. Water containment is provided by construction of exterior berms, interior berms, and overflow spillways, which are used to impound water during seasonal waterfowl migrations or to keep water out of the impounded area. Water supply may be provided by either river water or groundwater through the use of a pump station or well, respectively. Water control structures are utilized to maintain desired water elevations throughout the year. (UMRR Design Handbook, 2012)

title: 14  Notch
text: Spatial & Geometric Definition

title: 14  Notch
text:
Geometry Type: Polygon or Point (Notch_Geometry).
Spatial Delineation: Geometric cut, depression, or gap engineered into rock training structures, wing dams, closing dams, or earthen levee crests.
Cross-Sectional Typology: Trapezoidal, parabolic, or rectangular weir cuts.


Primary Restoration & Engineering Objectives

Secondary Channel Revitalization: Pass controlled baseflow through closing dams to refresh side channels without destabilizing main-channel navigation drafts.
Bathymetric Scour Generation: Concentrate localized flow vectors through the notch throat, carving deep downstream plunge pools (10 to 25 ft deep) that function as prime overwintering fish holes.
Sediment Purging: Re-energize sediment transport capacity through backwaters to purge deposited silt plugs.



Typical Cross-Sections, Dimensions & Sizing Criteria

Throat Widths: Bottom widths typically range from 10 to 50 ft; side slopes cut at 1V:2H to 1V:3H.
Depth of Invert: Invert set 1.0 to 4.0 ft below the parent weir crest or normal flat pool elevation.
Hydraulic Conveyance: Sized using broad-crested weir formulas (Q=C d LH 3/2 ) to restrict diverted river discharge to calibrated project thresholds (typically <5% of total channel discharge).



Construction & Implementation Methodology

Marine Excavation: Existing stone removed using barge-mounted hydraulic excavators equipped with rock buckets or heavy clamshells.
Bed & Abutment Armoring: Installing heavy riprap transitions along notch edges and lining the downstream plunge impact zone with Class IV–V stone to halt headcut unraveling.



Quality Control, Inspection & Long-Term Maintenance

Single-Beam Sonar Soundings: Annual hydrographic cross-sections through the notch and downstream scour basin to verify that scour hole depth remains stable and does not undermine the main weir abutments.

title: 14  Notch
text:
Spatial Feature Attribute

Definition
A notch is a deliberate opening cut into a riverine flow structure or levee (typically a dike) used to control the flow of water into and out of a low-flow area or adjacent floodplain.


Purpose
A notch creates a controlled gap or opening in the structure. Its purpose is to regulate water flow, manage river levels, and prevent damage from excessive water buildup. Notching can support flow regulation, sediment management, habitat creation, and flood control by selectively passing water and sediment and reconnecting channels and floodplains.


Applicability
Notches are applicable where targeted hydraulic connections are needed between the main channel and backwaters, side channels, or floodplain areas. They are commonly used to improve habitat, reduce sedimentation, restore natural inundation patterns, and modify river training structures or levees to better meet environmental objectives within Upper Mississippi River System (UMRS) restoration projects. (UMRR Design Handbook, 2012)

text: Spatial & Geometric Definition

title: 15  Pump Station
text:
Geometry Type: Point or Polygon (Pump_Station_Structure).
Spatial Delineation: Footprint encompassing cast-in-place concrete wet-wells, intake bays, discharge manifolds, electrical control buildings, and fuel/power infrastructure.
Operational Classification: High-capacity, low-head axial-flow pumping systems.


Primary Restoration & Engineering Objectives

Hydrologic Independence: Allow rapid filling or complete dewatering of moist soil units and managed wetland cells regardless of ambient river flood or drought stages.
Dewatering Reliability: Drain impounded areas during spring flood stages when external river levels sit higher than the internal wetland ground elevation.
Rapid Flood Protection: Evacuate internal runoff following heavy storm events to prevent premature drown-out of maturing wetland seed crops.



Typical Mechanical & Structural Engineering Specifications

Pumping Capacity: Total station flow capacities range between 2,000 and 25,000 gpm (5 to 55 cfs), operating against total dynamic heads (TDH) of 6 to 18 ft.
Pump Mechanics: Vertical axial-flow or mixed-flow electric submersible or lineshaft pumps. Sized with variable frequency drives (VFD) for adjustable flow rates.
Reversible Manifold Piping: Multi-valve directional piping manifolds allowing a single pump train to draw water from the river to fill the cell, or draw from the cell to discharge out into the river.



Construction & Implementation Methodology

Deep Foundation Systems: Reinforced concrete substructure founded on steel H-piling or driven ductile iron piles keyed into underlying load-bearing river sands to resist uplift hydrostatic pressures.
Cofferdam Dewatering: Wet-well construction executed within sheetpile cofferdams dewatered by deep-well point systems.



Quality Control, Inspection & Long-Term Maintenance

Intake Screening: Trash racks equipped with automated mechanical rakes or heavy bar screens (2- to 3-in clear spacing) to prevent log and debris ingestion.
Winterization: Annual late-autumn dewatering of pump bowls, lubrication checks, and cycling of emergency backup diesel generators under full load.

title: 15  Pump Station

Definition
A pump station is a facility that pumps water between two storage areas, a storage area and a river reach, or between different river reaches. It can also be used to transfer water within the same 2D Flow Area or between different cells within the same 2D Flow Area.


Purpose
Pump stations are used to introduce or remove water from backwater lakes, MSMUs, or other project areas using surface water (typically from a river) or groundwater. They provide controlled water level management, allowing project operators to manipulate hydrologic conditions to support habitat objectives, flood risk management, and operational needs.


Applicability
Pumping stations are used for removal of interior drainage from areas protected by local flood protection works and for water supply. Pumping stations can and should have negligible adverse environmental impacts. They can also be used to connect pumps, lift flows from lower to higher elevations, increase pressure in gravity flow distribution systems, and improve the selection and operation of water level management facilities within restoration projects. (UMRR Design Handbook, 2012)

Geometry Type: Polygon or Polyline(Revetment_Armor_Band).
Spatial Delineation: Armored protective blanket placed along littoral shoreline banks, island provar edges, wing dam abutments, and channel margins.
Materials: Heavy quarried angular stone riprap, crushed aggregate bedding, and non-woven geotextile filter fabric.


Primary Restoration & Engineering Objectives

Shoreline Erosion Arrest: Neutralize high hydraulic shear stresses (τ=γRS) induced by commercial towboat propeller wash, vessel wakes, and flood currents.
Wind-Wave Dissipation: Protect constructed earthen island fills and natural delta edges from wind-fetch wave impact and slumping.
Littoral Micro-Cover: Stone voids provide interstitial refuge and feeding zones for macroinvertebrates and small fish species.



Typical Cross-Sections, Dimensions & Sizing Criteria

Armor Sizing: USACE Class II to Class IV stone riprap (d 50 =12 to 18 in; top weight up to 1,500 lbs).
Blanket Thickness: 1.5× to 2.0× the d 100 stone size (typically 18 to 30 in thick).
Slope Geometry: Maximum stable slope angle is 1V:2H (1V:3H preferred).
Toe Key-In: Armored toe trench excavated 3.0 to 5.0 ft into the channel bed, or a wide stone launching apron (5 to 10 ft wide) designed to self-launch and protect the bank toe against scour.



Construction & Implementation Methodology

Marine Placement: Work conducted via spud barges using long-reach excavators equipped with hydraulic stone grapples or clamshell buckets to place stone smoothly without tearing geotextile.
Filter Layer Installation: High-survivability non-woven geotextile placed under the stone to stop fine-grained subgrade soils from leaching out through riprap voids.



Quality Control, Inspection & Long-Term Maintenance

Gradation Testing: Quarry riprap testing per ASTM standards to ensure durability, bulk specific gravity (≥2.60), and resistance to freeze-thaw cycles.
Post-Flood Audits: Boat-based visual and sonar scans to detect riprap displacement, toe undermining, or ice plucking along the waterline.

title: 16  Revetment
text:
Spatial Feature Attribute

Definition
A revetment is a cover or facing of erosion-resistant material placed directly on an existing slope, embankment, or dike. Unlike seawalls, revetments are not self-supporting and depend on the underlying soil for support.


Purpose
Revetments are used to stabilize river banks and protect shorelines from strong waves and currents. Bank revetments prevent erosion, maintain a stable channel, and support new habitat creation. (UMRR Design Handbook, 2012)


Applicability
The primary forces that affect shorelines are river currents and wind-driven wave action; ice action and waves created by towboats or recreational boats can also cause erosion. Revetment stabilization techniques can be employed singly or in combination to protect shoreline and add habitat diversity. Gradual side slopes and sand or mud soils can benefit turtles and waterbirds that nest, feed, and loaf on shorelines. Native plantings can be more aesthetically pleasing than traditional riprap, and traditional stabilization techniques can be refined (e.g., larger and mixed-grade rock) to improve habitat diversity for fish and invertebrates. (Report to Congress, 2004)


Notes
Restoration features now have a Program_UID field to distinguish between NESP and UMRR features. Aliases without program identification will be created for any field that currently has UMRR in the name, so they can be used for NESP or UMRR data.

title: 17  River Flow Structure
text:
Geometry Type: Polygon (Flow_Structure_Polygon).
Spatial Delineation: 3D structural stone footprint resting on the riverbed, representing river training dikes, chevrons, bendway weirs, closing dams, and hard-points.
Structural Material: 100% quarried limestone/dolomite riprap and stone core.


Primary Restoration & Engineering Objectives

Channel Steering & Velocity Partitioning: Direct river discharge into primary navigation lines while partitioning secondary flows into restoration backwaters.
Scour Hole Generation: Carve deep structural aquatic habitat niches through localized flow acceleration around structure tips and heads.
Island & Shoreline Sheltering: Act as rigid upstream hydrodynamic deflection shields protecting soft downstream wetland deposits.



Typical Cross-Sections, Dimensions & Sizing Criteria

Crest Widths: 6.0 to 12.0 ft along the top weir crest.
Side Slopes: Heavy stable stone slopes of 1V:1.5H to 1V:2H.
Crest Elevation: Range from submerged low sills (1.0 to 3.0 ft below pool) up to emergent structures (2.0 to 5.0 ft above normal pool).
Structural Prow / Nose: Heavily reinforced rounded apex with stone sizing upgraded to Class V (d 50 ≥24 in) to withstand direct river ice sheets.



Construction & Implementation Methodology

Marine Derrick Operations: Heavy rock barges positioned with tugboats; stone placed using clamshell buckets or hydraulic excavators working against river currents.
Upstream Root Tie-In: Structure landward roots deeply keyed into adjacent banks (15 to 30 ft) to prevent high-water flanking.



Quality Control, Inspection & Long-Term Maintenance

Acoustic Bathymetric Scans: Side-scan and multi-beam hydrographic surveys monitoring bed scour development and verifying structural mass stability.

Definition
River Flow Structure polygon is a natural or man-made flow (or sediment) control structure in a water course or water body such as a dike or weir. This feature should not be used to model a levee. Riverine flow structures, also called “river training structures,” are man-made constructions designed to modify the flow of a river, typically to control erosion, manage sediment transport, improve navigation, protect riverbanks, and sometimes enhance aquatic habitats by influencing water flow dynamics within the river channel.


Applicability
Training structures can be used to alter hydrodynamic conditions, the sediment transport regime, and ultimately habitat conditions on the UMRS. The 2010 EMP Report to Congress described how river training structures meet UMRS Environmental Objectives by improving fish habitat and water quality, stabilizing eroding channels, reducing sediment load to backwaters by reducing flow velocities, and maintaining water temperature and rock substrate. Crest Alignment Verification: High-precision RTK or lidar scans along the exposed crest during low-flow river stages to confirm structure crest stability.

title: 19  Water Control Structure
text:
Geometry Type: Point or Polygon (Water_Control_Structure_Location).
Spatial Delineation: Footprint encompassing reinforced concrete headwalls, drop inlets, culvert barrels, slide gates, stoplog bays, and energy dissipation aprons.
Structural Typology: Gravity flow stoplog structures, flap-gated culverts, screw-jack sluice gates, and radial gates.


Primary Restoration & Engineering Objectives

Water Surface Regulation: Provide bi-directional water-level control across moist soil cells, backwater lakes, and floodplain basins.
Bi-directional Flow Management: Retain managed pools during low river stages, permit rapid gravity drainage, and allow controlled gravity inflow during high-water pulses.
Fish Passage Control: Incorporate low-velocity bays or operational settings that permit native fish ingress while blocking rough fish (common carp).



Typical Structural & Hydraulic Engineering Criteria

Stoplog Bays: Multi-bay reinforced concrete structures (4 to 6 ft bay widths) with embedded stainless steel or aluminum slide channels housing treated timber or structural aluminum stoplogs.
Culvert Barrels: Heavy-duty reinforced concrete pipe (RCP) or structural aluminum/HDPE conduits (24 to 48 in diameter) passing through embankment bodies.
Seepage Cutoff Collars: Minimum of two concrete anti-seep collars or bentonite cutoff rings placed around culvert barrels within the embankment core to prevent internal seepage piping.
Scour Dissipation Aprons: Concrete stilling basins or Class III riprap aprons underlain by geotextile at structure outlets to absorb exit velocities (v>5.0 ft/s).



Construction & Implementation Methodology

Cast-in-Place Concrete Construction: Structural concrete engineered with minimum 28-day compressive strengths of f c′ ≥4,000 psi and air-entrainment (5% to 8%) for extreme freeze-thaw durability.
Sheetpile Cutoff Walls: Steel sheetpile cutoff walls driven 10 to 20 ft beneath concrete aprons to prevent under-seepage and structural piping.



Quality Control, Inspection & Long-Term Maintenance

Stoplog Seal Integrity: Annual inspection of stoplog rubber seals, lifting tracks, and slide gate screw-jacks. Lubrication of gear assemblies and clearing of silt accumulation within stoplog guide slots.

title: 19  Water Control Structure
text:
Spatial Features Attributes

Definition
Water control structures are structures within a water management system that convey water, control the direction or rate of flow, maintain a desired water surface elevation, or measure water levels or flows.


Purpose
Water control structures are used to regulate water levels, flow rates, and distribution within managed areas such as MSMUs, backwater lakes, and wetlands. They can be used to maintain or increase water depths to create open water areas, periodically drain or flood wetlands to enhance plant germination, and provide operational flexibility to meet multiple habitat objectives (e.g., for waterfowl, shorebirds, wading birds, reptiles, amphibians, and fisheries).


Applicability
Water control structures are applicable wherever active water level or flow management is required in Upper Mississippi River System (UMRS) restoration projects. They are commonly used to manage wetlands, backwaters, and managed floodplain units, and are integral components of water level management strategies implemented under HREP/UMRR projects. (UMRR Design Handbook, 2012)

title: 20  Well
text:
Geometry Type: Point (Groundwater_Well_Location).
Spatial Delineation: Point location of the drilled wellhead, surface sanitary seal, power connection, and discharge connection pipe.
Hydrogeologic Target: Deep unconsolidated alluvial sand and gravel aquifers within the modern river floodplain.


Primary Restoration & Engineering Objectives

Sediment-Free Water Delivery: Supply clean, silt-free groundwater to moist soil units, eliminating the high turbidity and sediment loads inherent to river surface water.
Drought-Proof Water Supply: Provide reliable filling capacity for managed waterfowl impoundments during severe late-summer droughts when river stages are depressed.
Winter Open-Water Maintenance: Discharge warm groundwater (50 ∘ F to 55 ∘ F) into impoundment pockets during midwinter freezes to maintain open-water foraging zones for wintering waterfowl.



Typical Hydrogeologic & Mechanical Specifications

Drilling Depths: Typically drilled 80 to 250 ft into basal alluvial gravel formations.
Casing & Screen Geometry: Heavy-duty steel or PVC casing (12 to 20 in diameter) with continuous-slot stainless steel well screens (0.040- to 0.080-in slot sizes) sized to match aquifer grain-size distributions.
Gravel Pack: Graded silica sand/gravel filter pack placed around the screen to stop fine sand intrusion.
Yield & Mechanics: High-capacity line-shaft or submersible turbine pumps delivering yields of 1,000 to 4,000 gpm (2.2 to 8.9 cfs).



Construction & Implementation Methodology

Mud-Rotary or Reverse-Circulation Drilling: Boreholes drilled into unconsolidated alluvium using heavy truck-mounted drilling rigs.
Well Development: High-energy surge-block surging, air-jetting, and continuous over-pumping until discharge water tests free of suspended sand grains (<5 mg/L).



Quality Control, Inspection & Long-Term Maintenance

Step-Drawdown Aquifer Testing: 24- to 72-hour continuous pump tests to establish baseline specific capacity (gpm/ft of drawdown) and ensure long-term sustainability without well-field interference.
Water Quality Testing: Routine chemical analysis testing for dissolved iron, manganese, and total dissolved solids (TDS) to track potential screen encrustation.

title: 20  Well
text:
Spatial Feature Attribute

Definition
A well is a shaft dug or drilled into the Earth for the purpose of extracting fluids from the subsurface, collecting environmental samples, injecting fluids into the subsurface, or extracting contamination or other impurities from the subsurface. Wells typically operate in conjunction with pumps and associated infrastructure.


Purpose
Wells are used to manage groundwater conditions, provide water supply, support environmental monitoring, and implement remediation or treatment measures in support of restoration projects. They enable controlled introduction or removal of water or other fluids, as well as sampling and observation, to inform design, operations, and adaptive management of project features.


Applicability
Water can be introduced or removed from a MSMU or backwater lake through the use of a well. The volume of water required will generally dictate whether a groundwater well can be feasibly constructed. Groundwater wells are limited in capacity due to available well yield from the aquifer, construction limitations, commercially available well pump size, and availability of utility power. Wells are applicable wherever groundwater interaction is a key component of water level management, habitat restoration, contaminant control, or environmental monitoring within Upper Mississippi River System (UMRS) restoration projects. title: 21  Wetland
text:
Geometry Type: Polygon (Wetland_Restoration_Polygon).
Spatial Delineation: Shallow-water aquatic marsh and bottomland wetland zones restored through grading, embankment construction, or river stage management.
Wetland Classes: Emergent hemi-marsh, deep-water marsh, scrub-shrub wetland, and wet meadow.


Primary Restoration & Engineering Objectives

Hemi-Marsh Restoration: Create balanced 50:50 ratios of dense emergent vegetation to open-water pools, maximizing wildlife diversity and nesting cover.
Nutrient & Silt Cycling: Serve as natural bio-retention filters that sequester suspended sediment, nitrogen, and phosphorus from passing floodwaters.
Amphibian & Reptile Nursery: Provide predator-sheltered, warm, sunlit nursery waters for amphibians, shorebirds, and native aquatic reptiles.



Typical Cross-Sections, Dimensions & Sizing Criteria

Water Depth Zonation:Littoral Shelf (0.0 to 1.0 ft depth): Supports emergent marsh species (Typha latifolia, Sagittaria latifolia, Scirpus spp.).
Intermediate Zone (1.0 to 3.0 ft depth): Promotes diverse beds of submersed aquatic vegetation (SAV) (Vallisneria americana, Potamogeton spp.).
Deep Pools (4.0 to 6.0 ft depth): Overwintering survival pockets for turtles and amphibians.
Micro-Topographic Diversity: Irregular curving shorelines, isolated mud islands, and variable bottom elevations to eliminate uniform bathymetry.



Construction & Implementation Methodology

Low-Ground-Pressure Earthmoving: Wide-track bulldozers (<3 psi ground pressure) shaping undulating bottoms and shallow perimeter benches.
Vegetation Transplants & Hydroseeding: Installation of pre-rooted emergent wetland plugs and broadcast wetland seed mixes immediately following final earthwork.



Quality Control, Inspection & Long-Term Maintenance

Hydro-Period Monitoring: Continuous pressure transducer stage recorders logging water depths throughout the year to confirm hydrologic permanence.
Invasive Species Eradication: Rigorous annual mechanical mowing and aquatic herbicide treatments targeting narrowleaf cattail and purple loosestrife.

title: 23  Dredging Placement
text: Spatial & Geometric Definition

title: 23  Dredging Placement
text:
Geometry Type: Polygon (Dredge_Placement_Site).
Spatial Delineation: Bounded footprint of upland disposal sites, confined disposal facilities (CDFs), in-water containment cells, or marsh nourishment zones receiving dredged sediments.
Placement Typology: Terrestrial containment basins, in-water island fill cells, marsh thin-layer nourishment zones, and beneficial-use stockpiles.


Primary Engineering & Operational Objectives

Dredged Material Retention: Securely hold thousands of cubic yards of slurried or mechanically excavated silts and sands without catastrophic containment failure.
Effluent Water Clarification: Allow sufficient detention settling time for hydraulic slurries to drop suspended solids, ensuring return water meets strict Clean Water Act Section 401 state water quality standards.
Beneficial Reuse & Topographic Elevation: Elevate low-lying floodplain terrains to create flood-refugia ridges, island cores, or agricultural soil enhancements.



Typical Cross-Sections, Dimensions & Sizing Criteria

Cell Capacities: Sized between 20,000 and 500,000+ cubic yards of material.
Perimeter Containment Dikes: Compacted earthen containment dikes (heights6 to 15 ft, side slopes 1V:3H) with minimum 3.0-ft interior freeboard.
Weir Dewatering Structures: Adjustable rectangular overflow weir boxes (morning-glory or stoplog weirs) sized to govern effluent decant rates based on Stokes’ Law hydraulic settling velocities.



Construction & Implementation Methodology

Hydraulic Discharge Management: Pipeline discharge placed at the furthest point from the overflow weir structure to maximize hydraulic residence time and particle settling.
Polymer / Flocculant Injection: When dredging fine colloidal clays, organic flocculants may be injected into the slurry line to accelerate settling.



Quality Control, Inspection & Long-Term Maintenance

Effluent Turbidity Monitoring: Continuous water testing at the weir discharge for Total Suspended Solids (TSS) and turbidity (NTU), maintaining compliance with state mixing-zone permits.
Dewatering & Crusting Management: Post-dredging trenching with specialized marsh excavators to promote rapid drying, desiccation, and soil consolidation.

title: 24  Borehole Points
text:
Geometry Type: Point (Geotechnical_Borehole_Point).
Spatial Delineation: Exact geographic surface coordinates of subsurface geotechnical exploration borings drilled during project investigation and design phases.
Associated Data Fields: Hole ID, surface ground elevation, depth to bedrock, depth to groundwater, sampling method, and laboratory test links.


Primary Engineering & Geotechnical Objectives

Subsurface Stratigraphy Profiling: Delineate alluvium strata, identify compressible soft organic clay/silt layers, and map bedrock depth.

Foundation Bearing Capacity Assessment: Determine in-situ shear strength, cohesion, and internal friction angles required to design stable embankments, concrete pump stations, and stone dikes.
Seepage & Settlement Modeling: Obtain soil samples for laboratory testing to calculate consolidation settlement (C c ​ ), compaction density, and hydraulic permeability (k).
Typical Drilling & Testing Specifications Drilling Methodology: Hollow-stem auger (HSA), mud-rotary drilling, or rock coring (NQ/HQ wireline barrels) deployed from truck rigs or marine spud barges.
Standard Penetration Testing (SPT): Conducted per ASTM D1586 at continuous 2.5- to 5.0-ft intervals, recording blow counts (N-values) with standard 140-lb split-spoon hammers.
Thin-Walled Shelby Tube Sampling: Undisturbed cohesive soil samples collected per ASTM D1587 for triaxial shear and consolidation testing.
Field Logging & Data Delivery Standard Boring Logs: Field logs classify all soil horizons according to the Unified Soil Classification System (USCS) (e.g., CH, CL, ML, SP, SM).
Grouting & Abandonment: All holes tremie-grouted from the bottom to the ground surface with high-solids bentonite slurry per state well abandonment regulations.
Quality Control & Long-Term Data Archiving Enterprise GIS Integration: All borehole logs digitized and georeferenced within the USACE MVR Geoportal database, preserving geotechnical baseline archives for future construction and maintenance.
