title: 25  Electrical Utility Node
text:
Geometry Type: Point (Electrical_Utility_Node).
Spatial Delineation: Point locations representing electrical infrastructure components powering restoration projects.
Component Types: Step-down transformers, primary utility metering poles, service disconnect panels, automatic transfer switches (ATS), backup diesel generators, motor control centers (MCC), and SCADA telemetry panels.


Primary Engineering & Operational Objectives

Power Supply & Conditioning: Deliver and step down commercial high-voltage power (480V, 3-phase) to operational voltage for high-capacity axial pumps, gate actuators, and lighting.
Automated System Control: House Programmable Logic Controllers (PLCs) and variable-frequency drives (VFDs) governing automated pumping regimes based on water level sensors.
Emergency Redundancy: Provide automatic generator startup within 10 seconds of commercial utility grid failure to protect facilities during flood events.



Technical & Electrical Engineering Specifications

Enclosure Standards: NEMA 4X stainless steel or heavy marine-grade aluminum enclosures to resist river corridor corrosion and moisture.
Elevated Platforms: All electrical equipment, MCCs, and generators mounted on structural steel platforms elevated minimum 2.0 to 3.0 ft above the 100-year Base Flood Elevation (BFE).
Surge & Lightning Protection: Industrial metal-oxide varistor (MOV) surge protection devices (SPDs) and copper grounding rod grids tied to all metallic structures.



Construction & Implementation Methodology

Utility Coordination: Point-of-service coordination with local commercial power utilities, extending single-phase or three-phase overhead/underground feeders to project boundaries.
Commissioning: Full load-bank testing of transformers and standby generators, megger testing of insulation on all pump motor leads, and telemetry testing with central control stations.



Quality Control, Inspection & Long-Term Maintenance

Infrared Thermography Scans: Annual thermal imaging scans of electrical panels under full pumping loads to detect hot spots, loose connections, or failing breaker contacts.

title: 26  Electrical Utility Segment
text: Spatial & Geometric Definition

title: 26  Electrical Utility Segment
text:
Geometry Type: Polyline (Electrical_Utility_Segment).
Spatial Delineation: Linear paths of underground, conduit-encased, aerial, or submarine electrical power distribution lines linking transformers to pumps and control nodes.
Structural Types: Direct-buried armored cables, concrete-encased duct banks, rigid galvanized steel (RGS) conduits, and aerial conductor spans.


Primary Engineering & Operational Objectives

Safe Power Distribution: Route electrical power across remote river floodplains, levee crests, and wetland environments without exposure to environmental or mechanical damage.
Subsurface Protection: Safeguard high-voltage feeder cables from burrowing rodents, flooding, seasonal frost heave, and maintenance grading.



Technical Specifications & Burial Depths

Underground Feeders: Copper conductors (THHN/THWN−2 or XHHW−2) sized to limit voltage drop to <3% at maximum continuous operating current.
Burial Depth Standards: Minimum burial depth of 36 to 48 in below finished grade.
Conduit Specification: Schedule 80 heavy-wall PVC conduits or rigid galvanized steel (RGS) where traversing roadways or embankment crossings.
Detectable Warning Ribbon: High-visibility red magnetic warning tape (“Caution: Buried Electric Line Below”) placed 12 in above conduits during trench backfill.



Construction & Implementation Methodology

Trenching & Horizontal Directional Drilling (HDD): Installed via open-cut trenching backfilled with compacted sand bedding, or HDD under existing levees and navigation channels to avoid disturbing structural embankments.



Quality Control, Inspection & Long-Term Maintenance

As-Built Traceability: All linear conduits and pull boxes mapped using sub-meter GPS prior to trench backfill.
Insulation Resistance Testing: Periodic high-potential (Hi-Pot) insulation testing to detect degradation of cable jackets exposed to high water tables.

title: 27  Feature Stationing
text:
Geometry Type: Point (Feature_Stationing_Point).
Spatial Delineation: Regular linear control points established along the alignment of an embankment centerline, access roadway, channel cut, or stone dike.
Format: Standard civil engineering linear stationing markers (0+00, 1+00, 5+00, etc.), where each station represents 100.0 linear feet.


Primary Engineering & Operational Objectives

Linear Coordinate Referencing: Establishes the authoritative linear measurement system used across all contract plan sheets, cross-sections, and inspection reports.
Asset Tracking & Work Measurement: Links geotechnical borings, culverts, spillway notches, and riprap armor transitions to an unambiguous linear coordinate along the structure.
Construction Progress Verification: Enables contract field inspectors to precisely verify contractor pay-application quantities based on physical station intervals.



Typical Specifications & Geometric Properties

Station Intervals: Points established every 100 ft on tangents and every 50 ft or 25 ft on horizontal curves.
Attribute Domains: Alignment Name, Station Number (XX+YY), Design Crest Grade, Left/Right Slope Offsets, and Elevation.



Survey & Layout Implementation

Staking Standards: Survey field crews install marked wooden hubs, iron pins, or aluminum caps during construction, tied to the project horizontal baseline.



Quality Control, Inspection & Long-Term Maintenance

Permanent Reference Hubs: Key stationing monuments (every 1,000 ft) cast into concrete markers or stamped brass disks to serve as permanent physical recovery points for post-flood inspection teams.

title: 27  Feature Stationing
text:
Spatial Feature Attributes

Definition
Feature Stationing: This refers to a system of linear referencing used to locate features along an alignment, such as an embankment or road. It is used for design, construction, and maintenance purposes. Reference points, generally expressed in linear units (typically feet), that allow identification of specific locations on engineered structures such as levees, control structures, roads, or walls.


Purpose
Feature stationing is used to tie design documents, construction records, inspections, and maintenance activities to precise locations along an engineered structure. By assigning station codes and associated elevations, project teams can consistently reference, locate, and document conditions, work items, or features along the structure.


Applicability
Feature stationing is applicable to any linear engineered feature within Upper Mississippi River System (UMRS) restoration projects where precise, repeatable location referencing is needed. Common examples include levees, floodwalls, spillways, roads, channels, and other structures where plans and profiles are based on stationing. (UMRR Design Handbook, 2012)

text: Spatial & Geometric Definition

title: 28  Pavement Section
text:
Geometry Type: Polygon (Pavement_Section_Footprint).
Spatial Delineation: Surface areas receiving engineered structural wearing courses across pump station staging yards, boat ramps, crest access roads, and parking turnarounds.
Surfacing Typology: Hot-mix asphalt (HMA), cast-in-place reinforced concrete pavement, and compacted crushed limestone aggregate surfacing.


Primary Engineering & Civil Objectives

Load-Bearing Surface: Support heavy maintenance vehicle loads (e.g., HS-20 truck loading: crane boom trucks, fuel tankers, and tractor-trailers) without rutting underlying subgrades.
Erosion & Overtopping Resistance: Prevent surface shear erosion on embankment crests and ramp approaches during controlled overtopping flood events.
All-Weather Operational Access: Ensure round-the-clock maintenance access to remote water control structures during heavy rain and flood-fighting operations.



Typical Structural Pavement Cross-Sections

Heavy-Duty Concrete (Pump Yards / Ramps): 8.0 to 10.0 in cast-in-place concrete (fc′ ≥4,000 psi) with epoxy-coated rebar mats, underlain by 6.0 in of crushed aggregate base over non-woven geotextile.
Crushed Aggregate Surfacing (Levee Roads): 6.0 to 8.0 in dense-graded crushed limestone road base (IDOT/WDOT dense-graded aggregate), compacted to ≥98% Standard Proctor density.
Cross-Slope Drainage: Crowned centerline or uniform cross-slope of 2.0% directing surface sheet flow into vegetated side swales.



Construction & Implementation Methodology

Subgrade Stabilization: Proof-rolling native subgrades; subgrade stabilization using biaxial geogrids where crossing soft alluvial clay strata.
Joint Sealants & Finishing: Concrete slabs scored with transverse contraction joints every 15 ft; silicone joint sealants applied to exclude water and freeze-thaw cracking.



Quality Control, Inspection & Long-Term Maintenance

Pavement Condition Audits: Annual inspections checking for surface rutting, washboarding, joint spalling, or subgrade settlement following flood inundation.

title: 28  Pavement Section

A pavement section is a portion of a pavement branch that differs in some aspect from other sections such that further segmentation is required to uniquely identify that section. text: Spatial & Geometric Definition

title: 29  Road Segment
text:
Geometry Type: Polyline (Road_Segment_Centerline).
Spatial Delineation: Linear centerlines of service corridors, levee crest roads, haul paths, and permanent public access roadways servicing restoration sites.
Data Fields: Road Name, Road Class (Maintenance Service vs. Public Access), Surface Material, Top Width, Design Speed, and Maximum Axle Load Rating.


Primary Engineering & Operational Objectives

Civil Network Connectivity: Form the continuous vehicular transportation network allowing USACE, USFWS, and State DNR personnel to access water control structures, pump stations, and habitat monitoring reaches.
Emergency Flood-Fighting Corridor: Serve as heavy haul routes for rock trucks and sandbagging operations during high-water river emergencies.



Typical Cross-Sections, Dimensions & Sizing Criteria

Roadway Widths: Crest service roads span 10.0 to 14.0 ft; two-way access roads span 20.0 to 24.0 ft.
Turnout Geometry: Passing turnouts (width20 ft, length 50 to 100 ft) established every 1,000 to 1,500 ft along single-lane levee roads.
Maximum Longitudinal Gradients: Grades held below 6% (approaches to levee crests restricted to <8%).



Construction & Implementation Methodology

Grading & Compaction: Motor graders establishing crowned profiles; heavy vibratory rollers sealing surface aggregates to shed rainfall without softening subgrades.
Culvert Crossings: Corrugated metal pipes (CMP) or dual-wall HDPE culverts (18 to 36 in) installed at low points with riprap flared end sections to ensure ditch conveyance.



Quality Control, Inspection & Long-Term Maintenance

Surface Regrading & Dust Abatement: Annual post-winter grading, spot aggregate replenishment, and application of calcium chloride dust palliatives near public trail intersections.

They are typically used to represent project access roads, levee-top roads, service roads, and internal circulation routes that provide construction, operations, maintenance, or public access. title: 31  Water Utility Node
text:
Geometry Type: Point (Water_Utility_Node).
Spatial Delineation: Geographic point locations representing discrete hydraulic fixtures, fittings, and mechanical control nodes within project water delivery systems.
Component Typology: Gate valves, butterfly valves, check valves, vacuum/air-relief valves, cleanouts, hydrants, flow meters, and manifold tee-junctions.


Primary Engineering & Hydraulic Objectives

Pipeline Flow Isolation: Enable operators to isolate, balance, or throttle flow rates across individual pipe legs within complex multi-cell wetland delivery systems.
Surge & Vacuum Protection: Air/vacuum relief valves release entrapped air pockets during pipeline filling and introduce air during rapid draining to prevent catastrophic vacuum pipeline collapse.
Volume Flow Metering: Ultrasonic or magnetic flow meters recording pumped water volumes for water-budget accounting and regulatory reporting.



Technical & Mechanical Specifications

Valving Specifications: Resilient-seated wedge gate valves or high-performance rubber-lined butterfly valves rated for minimum 150 psi working pressure.
Access Vaults: Underground nodes housed inside precast reinforced concrete utility vaults equipped with aluminum diamond-plate hatch doors (H−20 traffic-rated), interior drain sumps, and access ladders.
Corrosion Protection: All valves and fittings epoxy-coated per AWWA C550, with stainless steel assembly bolts and sacrificial zinc anode bags in corrosive alluvial soils.



Quality Control, Inspection & Long-Term Maintenance

Valve Exercising Programs: Semi-annual operational cycling of all buried and vault-housed valves through their complete open/close travel to prevent sediment binding.

title: 32  Water Utility Segment
text:
Geometry Type: Polyline (Water_Utility_Segment).
Spatial Delineation: Linear paths of pressurized supply pipes, gravity discharge lines, siphon tubes, and dewatering conduits linking pump stations, wells, and wetland cells.
Material Typology: High-density polyethylene (HDPE) DR-11/DR-17 pipe, ductile iron pipe (DIP), and reinforced concrete cylinder pipe (RCCP).


Primary Engineering & Hydraulic Objectives

Bulk Water Conveyance: Transport large volumes of water (5 to 50+ cfs) between river sources, wells, and isolated interior moist soil units across long distances.
Pressure Containment: Withstand sustained pumping operating heads, transient hydraulic water hammer surges, and external earth/vehicle loadings.
Embankment Integrity: Provide closed, continuous conveyance across or through earthen levees without inducing structural piping or seepage along pipe outer walls.



Technical Specifications & Hydraulic Sizing

Pipe Diameters: Sized between 12 and 48 in inside diameter based on fluid mechanics equations (Q=V⋅A), restricting internal velocities to 4.0 to 8.0 ft/s to minimize dynamic head loss.
Pipe Jointing: HDPE pipelines joined using continuous thermal butt-fusion welding per ASTM F2620, producing zero-leakage, fully restrained joint strings.
Anti-Seepage Measures: Where pipes penetrate through earthen levees, concrete cutoff collars, bentonite seepage rings, and impervious clay backfill are placed along the barrel.
Siphon Configurations: For over-the-levee pipelines, pipe crowns cross above the levee crest and feature vacuum-breaker valves at the high point to terminate siphon action.



Quality Control, Inspection & Long-Term Maintenance

Hydrostatic Pressure Testing: Pressure testing conducted per AWWA standards (e.g., testing at 1.5× working design pressure for 2 hours) prior to trench backfill.
Internal CCTV Video Inspections: Closed-circuit robotic crawler cameras run through pipe barrels at 5-year intervals to verify the absence of joint displacement, sediment plugs, or internal scaling.

text:
UMRS Restoration Features Database Crosswalk to UMRR and NESP Design Terminology
The UMRS Restoration Features database provides a common geospatial vocabulary for documenting, mapping, and managing ecosystem-restoration features across the Upper Mississippi River System (UMRS). It distinguishes between restoration features—such as DredgingEvent, Island, Wetland, Revetment, RiverineFlowStructure, and MoistSoilMgmtUnits—and restoration support features, such as DredgingPlacement, access infrastructure, utilities, stationing, and investigation points.
The database’s purpose is to translate varied project-design terminology into a consistent spatial data structure. A single design action may require multiple mapped database features. For example, a notched closure structure may be represented by RiverineFlowStructure or RiverineFlowStructureLine plus a Notch; an island created with dredged material may include DredgingEvent, DredgingPlacement, Island, and, where applicable, Wetland or Embankment.
This common structure allows UMRR and NESP projects to be mapped, queried, compared, and reported using the same feature classes while preserving each program’s established design terminology. The database does not replace the UMRR Environmental Design Handbook or the NESP Environmental Design Toolkit. Rather, it provides the spatial-data framework that connects their design measures to mapped project components.
Both programs should use the database feature classes as the authoritative mapped term, while retaining the original UMRR or NESP design term as a source attribute, alias, or project-description field.

UMRR
The UMRR Environmental Design Handbook contains detailed terminology for Habitat Rehabilitation and Enhancement Project (HREP) design, including shoreline and riverbank protection, localized water-level management, dredging, river-training structures and secondary-channel modifications, floodplain restoration, island design, aeration, and tributary restoration.
UMRR projects can use the database to convert these detailed design terms into standardized spatial features. For example:
Backwater and secondary-channel dredging can be mapped as DredgingEvent and, when an excavated channel remains, FlowChannel.
Dredged material used for island construction, wetlands, or topographic diversity can be mapped as DredgingPlacement and linked to Island, Wetland, or Embankment.
Closure structures, dikes, weirs, chevrons, wing dams, vanes, and rock sills can be mapped as RiverineFlowStructure or RiverineFlowStructureLine.
Wing-dam notches and notched closures can be mapped as Notch in association with the applicable riverine flow structure.
Shoreline protection and rock revetment can be mapped as Revetment.
Moist Soil Management Units can be mapped as MoistSoilMgmtUnits, with related Embankment, WaterControlStructure, PumpStation, Well, and water-utility support features.
Reforestation, wetland-species planting, and floodplain vegetation establishment can be mapped as FloraPlantingOrSeeding.
Depressional, emergent, and restored wetlands can be mapped as Wetland.
Barrier islands, seed islands, and other constructed islands can be mapped as Island or IslandLine, based on the project’s spatial representation.
Using the database allows UMRR to retain its detailed HREP design history while creating consistent feature-level mapping across projects, pools, reaches, and districts. It also supports analysis of where and how UMRR has implemented individual restoration measures over time. The UMRR handbook specifically recognizes that HREPs often combine multiple techniques to address complex habitat problems; the database captures those combinations as related mapped features instead of forcing the project into one broad label.


NESP
The NESP Environmental Design Toolkit provides planning-level design tools for five principal restoration-feature groups: shoreline stabilization, dredging, river-training structures and secondary-channel modifications, floodplain restoration, and islands. The toolkit uses design pamphlets, drawings, and parametric-cost tools to support early feature identification, alternative development, and plan formulation.
NESP projects can use the database to map proposed and constructed project components consistently with UMRR while retaining NESP’s planning and design terminology. For example:
Shoreline stabilization features, including rock revetments and related protective structures, can be mapped as Revetment.
Dredge cuts, fish-habitat dredging, and access dredging can be mapped as DredgingEvent; excavated conveyance areas can also be mapped as FlowChannel.
Beneficial use of dredged material, including placement for islands, berms, ridge-and-swale topography, or thin-layer placement, can be mapped as DredgingPlacement.
Chevrons, bullnoses, closure structures, guide structures, flow-diversion structures, and other river-training measures can be mapped as RiverineFlowStructure or RiverineFlowStructureLine.
Notched structures can be mapped as Notch and linked to the associated riverine flow structure.
Woody bundles and anchored or locked logs can be mapped as FishStructure when fish habitat is their primary purpose, or as a riverine flow structure when their primary purpose is flow or sediment management.
Potholes, depressional wetlands, emergent wetlands, and vegetation features can be mapped as Wetland and FloraPlantingOrSeeding.
Narrow islands, wide islands, rock-ring islands, seed islands, islands with berms, and islands with emergent wetlands can be mapped as Island, IslandLine, and associated Embankment or Wetland features.
The database gives NESP a consistent mechanism to carry planning-level feature concepts into design, mapping, cost estimating, project documentation, and future performance evaluation. NESP explicitly builds on information from prior UMRS projects and the UMRR Environmental Design Handbook; using the same spatial feature vocabulary supports that continuity.
